speaker: Unknown
quote_text: Okay, ready to go with it? Thank you. Ben,  congratulations on the win. Can we just ask for your opinion on the pitch? Obviously a lot  of talk about it, plenty of chat. Nice to win, but similar to Melbourne, I guess, the win there,  the short one, is it not ideal for you? God, yeah. Straight in there with the pitch rather  than the victory. Okay. We can go the other way around if you want. Yeah, that'd be nice. I think  there's two ways to look at it. I think for me, Test cricket, the reason why it's the best format  is because it presents its own challenges from one week to another. And this week we were presented  with conditions that were difficult, but we were playing against another team who had the exact  same conditions to come up against. And I thought the way that we identified the conditions quickly  and realised and committed to what we thought we needed to do as a team to give ourselves the best  chance of winning that game was very impressive. But then I think from the other side of it, from  a non-playing point of view, I get asked questions all the time about the longevity of this format.  People even say, like, saving Test cricket, which I think is a bit far. But for me, I think if  you're there on day one, you've had a great time, you've seen wickets falling, you've seen balls  flying off everywhere because there's a lot on offer and a lot of helpful conditions for the  bowling opposition. And then batters feel like they need to take a few more risks than they  normally would. So, with 16 wickets and 200 runs being scored, it's a good day out, especially  if you're in hospitality and the alcohol's free, so that's all good. But the game's played over  five days. Without a little bit of weather, it probably wouldn't have finished on day  four. So I think from someone who believes that Test cricket should and always will be  the best format and should never disappear, that's not ideal from that point of view. But from  a playing point of view and being in the dressing room, it's great that you get challenged. We might  have conditions that are completely different next week and we'll have to do the exact same thing,  which is assess those conditions quickly and come up with a plan as a team to execute plans and  a way of playing that we feel is going to give us the best chance of winning. No one means to.  It's tough for groundsmen. They're not actively coming out there and producing wickets that  are tricky and 16 wickets are falling in the day. So it's tough. But, yeah, I guess I get  asked all the time about what needs to happen, saving Test cricket, this, that and the other.  But when you see extreme conditions like that, that's not going to help the game in the future,  I don't think. But we won the game. We had to come up with a way as a team to do that and we did it.  Talk about that now, if you want, about the win. You made two sort of significant changes from the  winter, with Emilio at the top and bringing Ollie back. Both of those guys made a pretty chunky  contribution to getting this done. Just a word on both those guys coming in for the first time and  coming back into the team and helping England get a win. Yeah, obviously it was Emilio's debut  this week, and since we announced the squad, he knew for a while that on June 4th he would  be playing his first Test match for England. And Ollie's obviously played 20-odd Tests before  getting recalled to the squad this week. So, yeah, two guys probably feeling quite similar  emotions building up to it, and two guys who have made very important contributions to England  getting a win this week. I said to Emilio, that's at the high end of challenge as an opening  batter that you're going to be exposed to, so you're better off getting it early on so you can  understand how tough it is. And for him to make a significant contribution with the bat at the top  of the order, I think, will do wonders for his confidence and make him realise how hard that step  up can be. Opening the batting is always tough, and especially opening the batting in England can  be even tougher than anywhere else in the world. And I think this week he found that out, but he  came up with a way to score runs and was a huge reason as to why we were able to put a pretty  big total on the board for New Zealand to chase down. And, yeah, Ollie Robinson's skill has never  been in question. There's just a few other things that we'd obviously spoken about behind the scenes  that we wanted to see him go away and improve on, and he's obviously gone away and done that. But  the pleasing thing for me, I think, as a captain, as a leader in the group, is the way that he's  spoken about this week. It would be very easy to rest on your laurels when everything's gone so  well for him, but the language he's used around it being just the start, there's a lot more hard work  to put into it. And the more Ollie Robinson has an England shirt on his back, the better it is for us  because he's an outstanding bowler, and he showed that this week. On day one when those wickets were  falling, obviously Brook came up, you've seen that from him before. And then second innings, Duckett  and Smith were really proactive. Obviously you've had the experience of Perth and Melbourne in terms  of crapshoots to a point. Did that help, the fact that you know how these games tend to go? Again,  I think Perth compared to here were two completely different types of challenges. Perth was excessive  bounce, whereas at Lord's here it was variation of bounce up or down and quite excessive seam  movement. So, yeah, it was going to be tough to get your runs. I thought both bowling units bowled  very, very well on that pitch, but I thought the way that we committed to trying to score off  anything that was slightly loose on this wicket is what allowed us to get up to a 250-run lead  because we knew that we weren't going to get that many scoring opportunities from this New Zealand  attack, who were so relentless in their plans and execution. And we knew we had to capitalise  on anything that was presented to us to score because in between that was going to be tough.  Same with our bowling group. If you look at the two disciplines of the game, I think it was our  bowling that really was the biggest contributor to winning this week. It was our relentlessness with  our execution of plans. We had them all nailed down coming into this week and I thought we just  executed what we wanted to do for longer periods of time than New Zealand wanted to, probably in  those conditions that we were both presented with. Nathan was just in here before you. He said that  Phillips' innings today showed perhaps they got it wrong, that they should have grafted more.  Were you surprised that they were...? Again, it's all hindsight, I guess. You've got to commit  to something. You've got to commit to what you decide to do. I think it's only ever right or  wrong depending on if it's successful or not. Being half-hearted with something that you decide  to do is probably not the way forward. But, yeah, having someone like Glenn down in that middle  order, who's quite an aggressive player, I think that just suits his natural game. And you've got  some of the guys at the top of the order with New Zealand whose natural game isn't what Glenn's is.  So again, conditions can suit players more or less depending on what they are, if that makes sense.  Will, Stefan, and we'll take one more after that. Oh, sorry, Mel first. Apologies. Go on. Just  before a Test series, first Test series at the time, there's always a sense of questioning and  speculation about selection, players coming in, how they might play, players returning in  this case and also coming back from injury, the way the whole team is going to play. All of  this has been playing out in light of what has happened over the last six months. But in a Test  match like that, do you feel you got answers to a lot of the things that were unknowns before coming  in, or is it one where you think it was so unusual that maybe everyone needs to just kind of wait  for another couple of Tests so you can actually perhaps see in different kinds of circumstances,  if that makes sense? No, not really. All you can do is prepare as well as you can. We had  three days at Loughborough as a team before, doing some pretty high-intensity training  together, because normally how it's worked in the past is that we don't meet up as a team  until three or four days before the Test match, and then everyone's so buzzing and excited to get  going that it's all a bit helter-skelter, if that makes sense. Everyone's wanting to do so much when  they first get here and the emotions are flying, whereas I sort of wanted to get all that kind of  stuff done and dusted a week before the Test match started, especially with everything that had  been going on the six months before. So, look, we prepared incredibly well for this New Zealand  team. It's very useful having Brendon as coach, Tim as someone who's played a lot of cricket with  pretty much all of that New Zealand team. So we knew the plans that we needed to go into to expose  the New Zealand batting group's weaknesses. So, yeah, we were as well prepared as we  possibly could be before this game started, and then we were able to execute those plans that  we spoke about and were putting into practice well in advance of this game starting. So, again, just  because the conditions were a bit extreme doesn't mean that we have to sit back and wait to see  if things are going to suit any type of agenda that's been going on at the moment. We came here  to win this game this week and we did that. Ben, just to expand on the future of Test cricket stuff  and pitches like this, do you think that pitches like this would put off both players and fans of  the longest format? Is that what you're saying? No, I didn't say that at all, Will, so don't put  words in my mouth, please. We played here last year against India and that was sort of completely  different, where it was a little bit harder to get your rewards as a bowler. But it ended up being a  great Test match because it got to day five and it went the distance. But I think the modern psyche  towards Test cricket is that both teams want to win. They don't want to sort of drag it out and  just see where it ends up. I think both teams, when they play against each other, are always  thinking about what move are we going to make to win this Test match, whether that be from day two,  day three, day four. Again, my thing about that is if you buy tickets to day one on that, you've had  a great day, might wake up with a sore head on day two because it's just so exciting. But as the game  prolongs itself, the game's done by day three, day four, day five. That's not good for Test cricket.  It's played over five days. You want the cricket to be played over as much of the time as possible.  And again, without rain, that's probably not going to happen this week. And that's just my take on  the whole thing about wickets that offer so much. What is the right word? Inconsistency. Thank you,  whoever whispered that, because that's what it was. It was an inconsistent pitch. No one's fault.  No one's meant to do it. But it's tough because as a batter, you just never feel in. You're not sure  what's going to happen off the wicket and then that presents more chance as a bowler. You then  have to change the way that you might play as a batting group and it's tough. But again, we could  turn up next week and the game goes five days and it could be a draw and then everyone goes, this  pitch is too flat. So it's so tough to get it right. But, yeah, I just think the wickets is  something that I think can help towards the understanding of what needs to help Test cricket  stay around. It's not just a case of players have lost the ability to dig in, to stick in and all  that kind of stuff. Such an easy thing to say, but, yeah, put your pads on and go out there  and face Ollie Robinson if you want. Stefan. You and Brendon have always tried to get across  the message about how enjoyable it should be to play cricket. It was noticeable this week,  smiles on faces, the atmosphere. You touched on how impressive the guys were when they spoke  pre-match. How enjoyable has this week been for you personally and the team coming through a  time that maybe wasn't quite so enjoyable? Yeah, it was good. I'm not going to lie. Obviously very,  very happy that we won this week. I knew how big this game was in terms of the result and how it  was going to be perceived externally if it didn't go well. But now it's gone well, I probably won't  be real happy and smiling until I get up there and share a proper beer with the boys because  it's like, I have to come here and do this. No disrespect to you guys, but it's like, get that  out of the way and then it'll be all right. But as I said about Ollie before, it would  be easy for him to rest on his laurels, and I'm sort of the same. It's like, right, we've  won the first game of the summer. It's great that we've managed to do it, but we've got five more to  go. We've got two more games against New Zealand, who are a quality team. We always have great  battles against them. So, look, we're one Test match down out of six, so there's a long way to  go still. Loads of questions about criticism and all that stuff. Just going into this Test match,  did you think that any sort of win will do? Well, you're winning, yeah, yeah, yeah. I don't think  people care, really. It always helps. That's always nice. There's no negative to winning. Okay,  you're done. Thank you. Thanks. Cheers, guys.
title: STOKES: “DON’T PUT WORDS IN MY MOUTH, PLEASE!”  England beat New Zealand by 115 runs
